content_text:
Hydro brings high-recycled aluminium to General Motors EV with Hydro CIRCAL
General Motors’ Cadillac OPTIQ will feature a front bumper system made with Hydro CIRCAL, an advanced aluminium alloy composed of at least 75 percent post‑consumer scrap produced at Hydro’s newest U.S. recycling facility in Cassopolis, Michigan.
The 2026 Cadillac OPTIQ with Hydro CIRCAL recycled aluminium. (Photo: General Motors) 
Hydro, automotive supplier Shape Corp. and General Motors are demonstrating how aluminium from end-of-life products can be recycled and returned to new automotive applications, supporting increased circularity in the mobility sector.
The collaboration marks one of the first U.S. implementations of Hydro CIRCAL in a structural, safety‑critical automotive application.
“By bringing recycled aluminium back into demanding vehicle applications, we can reduce embedded emissions, strengthen material circularity and make better use of the resources already in circulation,” says Duncan Pitchford, Vice President Recycling, Hydro Aluminum Metal.
High-recycled aluminium for automotive applications
Hydro will supply Hydro CIRCAL from its U.S. recycling facility in Cassopolis, Michigan. Shape Corp. will engineer and assemble the front bumper system to GM specifications, with integration into the Cadillac OPTIQ platform.
By sourcing recycled aluminium locally and making it in Michigan, GM strengthens U.S. production and supply chain resilience while demonstrating how regional recycling networks can return valuable materials to new vehicle applications.
Hydro CIRCAL uses aluminium recovered from end-of-life products such as vehicles, windows, doors and electrical cables. The material is remelted and transformed into new aluminium products through Hydro's recycling operations.
Illustration showing the front bumper beam, a crash-management component, positioned at the front of the vehicle. General Motors has selected Hydro CIRCAL for this application in the Cadillac OPTIQ. 
The product offers a market-leading carbon footprint of 1.5 kg CO₂e per kg of aluminium, or lower, while meeting demanding automotive requirements for strength, energy absorption, corrosion resistance and formability. The low carbon footprint means Hydro CIRCAL delivers an estimated 70 percent reduction in CO₂ emissions compared to the North American average for primary aluminium production.
How the component is used
The front bumper beam is a structural crash‑management part located at the front of the vehicle, behind the visible bumper cover. It absorbs and distributes impact energy in collisions to help protect passengers, pedestrians and critical EV systems, an application where material choice is essential.
Using Hydro CIRCAL in this part demonstrates that aluminum with high post‑consumer recycled content can meet demanding performance needs while helping lower embedded carbon footprint.
About Hydro CIRCAL
Hydro CIRCAL is Hydro’s recycled aluminium product line containing a minimum 75 percent post‑consumer scrap with third‑party (DNV) verification. Each batch carries verified documentation to support customer traceability and reporting. In North America, Hydro produces Hydro CIRCAL at its U.S. recycling operations, including Cassopolis, Michigan.

Cell therapy weekly: FDA approves glycogen storage disease type 1a gene therapy
20 Aug 2026 
Written by Kadeja Johnson 
Disease area 
FDA 
Gene therapy 
News 
Regulation & policy 
The week in cell therapy 
This week: Sangamo Therapeutics (CA, USA) auctions off its main assets, Andelyn Biosciences (OH, USA) and Queen’s University (Ontario, Canada) partner to advance a lysosomal storage disorder gene therapy program and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA; MD, USA) approves a gene therapy for glycogen storage disease type 1a (GSD1a).
The news highlights:
Sangamo completes auctions of main assets 
Partnership to advance gene therapy program for lysosomal storage disorder 
FDA approves glycogen storage disease type 1a gene therapy 
Sangamo completes auctions of main assets
In June 2026, Sangamo Therapeutics announced plans to sell its assets through voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings to maximize stakeholder value. Nearly two months later, the company has successfully concluded the auction process, selecting winning bids totaling approximately US$163.55 million in cash at closing, plus up to US$100 million in potential future milestone payments.
During a court-supervised auction process:
PTC Therapeutics (NJ, USA) acquired Sangamo’s Fabry disease program, ST-920, for US$111 million cash, plus up to US$100 million in milestone payments upon receiving traditional or full approval from the FDA.
Eli Lilly and Company (IN, USA) purchased Sangamo’s capsid delivery, zinc finger and modular integrase platforms, plus the prion disease program, ST-506, for US$50 million cash.
Various bidders secured Sangamo tools and equipment for US$2.55 million cash considerations at closing
“Reaching the conclusion of this first competitive auction represents an important milestone in Sangamo’s reorganization,” said Sandy Macrae, CEO of Sangamo. “Our priority has been to seek value-maximizing transactions for all stakeholders, and we are pleased that our platform technologies, Fabry disease and prion programs attracted strong interest from parties who have the scale to continue their development for patients in need. We remain focused on monetizing our remaining assets and seeking Court approvals to finalize all sales.”
Read more 
Partnership to advance gene therapy program for lysosomal storage disorder
Andelyn Biosciences and Queen’s University have partnered to develop and manufacture AAV9-GM2, a gene therapy indicated for GM2 gangliosidosis. GM2 gangliosidosis is a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder, progressively destroying nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. GM2 is caused by genetic mutations that disrupt normal lysosomal function, leading to the buildup of harmful substances in cells and severe decline in neurological abilities.
This partnership aims to advance AAV9-GM2 by leveraging Andelyn’s AAV Curator® Platform. Commenting on the partnership, Matt Niloff, Andelyn’s Chief Commercial Officer, spoke on how the company is “proud to partner with Queen’s University to advance this gene therapy candidate for the benefit of patients and families facing the challenges of GM2 gangliosidoses.”
Continuing, Niloff reflected on the company’s commitment to support innovative gene therapy programs targeting rare and ultra-rare diseases, stating:
“Our deep expertise in AAV development and production allows us to support Queen’s University with the scale and quality rigor necessary to bring this life-changing therapy one step closer to reality.”
Read more 
FDA approves glycogen storage disease type 1a gene therapy
The FDA has granted accelerated approval for GENGLYCOS™ – a gene therapy developed by Ultragenyx Pharmaceuticals (CA, USA) – in adult and pediatric patients eight years and older with GSD1a. GSD1a, an ultra-rare genetic metabolic disorder, is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase-alpha, reducing the liver’s ability to release glucose into the bloodstream. Patients with this disorder require nutritional management consisting of raw cornstarch intake as an oral glucose replacement therapy.
“The approval of GENGLYCOS fulfills our commitment to provide the first therapy that directly targets the root cause of GSD1a. The reduced reliance on cornstarch, experienced by patients in our clinical studies, demonstrates this gene therapy’s ability to establish the normal breakdown of glycogen to produce glucose during fasting or episodes of metabolic stress. This ability to regulate glucose has alleviated the disease burden and has the potential to mitigate the risk of severe or life-threatening hypoglycemia for these patients,” commented Ultragenyx’ chief medical offer, Eric Crombez. “As our first gene therapy approval, GENGLYCOS represents an important achievement for our company and the realization of the promise of a powerful new tool to deliver transformative medicines for people living with rare diseases.”

Merck-Moderna cancer vaccine win spurs stock jump, speculation of Keytruda-like impact
By
Nick Paul Taylor 
Aug 20, 2026 9:25am 
Merck & Co. 
Moderna 
cancer vaccine 
Keytruda 
Analysts have predicted Moderna could book $5.4 billion in intismeran sales in melanoma by 2040. (James Waldron)
As the dust settles on a phase 3 announcement that added $45 billion to Moderna’s market cap, analysts have begun to ask a question that could define cancer care in the coming years: can use of the vaccine be as broad as Keytruda?
Moderna’s share price closed up 177% on Wednesday following the disclosure of a topline win from a phase 3 trial of its Merck & Co.-partnered cancer vaccine. Analysts at Evercore ISI and William Blair cited the involvement of retail investors and short sellers, respectively, as factors in the surge—but that only partly explains the jump. Shares in Merck, which has a much larger market cap, closed up almost 13%. 
The stock increases reflect the potential for the cancer vaccine, intismeran autogene, to work in settings beyond the adjuvant melanoma indication covered by Wednesday’s INTerpath-001 update. Sales in adjuvant melanoma could exceed $2 billion, Guggenheim Securities analysts said, but broader use will be needed to justify Moderna and Merck’s newly inflated valuations. 
As William Blair analysts noted, the debate among investors “will now turn to how much the INTerpath-001 data have de-risked intismeran in other cancer settings and if this product can be as broad as Keytruda.” 
Merck grew annual Keytruda sales to north of $30 billion by validating the checkpoint inhibitor in a long list of indications. Last month, David Berman, M.D., Ph.D., chief development officer at Moderna, told investors there is “increased reason to believe” that intismeran will work against diseases vulnerable to Keytruda. 
The “big question,” Berman said at the time, is whether intismeran works outside those settings. 
Analysts have generated towering sales estimates even without factoring in the potential for intismeran to work in settings where checkpoint inhibitors have struggled, such as pancreatic cancer. Based on the phase 3 success, William Blair analysts predicted Moderna could book $5.4 billion in intismeran sales in melanoma by 2040 under its 50-50 profit-share agreement with Merck.
The analysts’ Moderna model for 2040 now includes sales of $10 billion in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and sales of $3.3 billion in renal cell carcinoma (RCC). In RCC, the analysts see “upside potential ... pending more effective therapies in this high-unmet-need indication.” 
Merck and Moderna are running nine phase 2 and 3 trials, providing opportunities beyond melanoma, NSCLC and RCC.
For Moderna, the studies represent a chance to diversify beyond its flatlining COVID-19 vaccine business. The trials are key to Merck too, with Guggenheim analysts noting that intismeran could be an important part of the drugmaker’s growth “as it works to navigate through biosimilar and pricing pressure for Keytruda starting later this decade.” Keytruda could face biosimilar competition in 2028.
The next question is whether the excitement survives a look at the full data from the adjuvant melanoma trial. Merck and Moderna need a hazard ratio of 0.65 or lower to clearly differentiate intismeran, William Blair analysts said. A hazard ratio above 0.75 would underwhelm the analysts, who cautioned that the share price moves in “substantially more conviction than the data disclosed thus far supports.”
Multiple companies could be hit by the fallout if the phase 3 numbers underwhelm. The share prices of Arcturus Therapeutics and BioNTech closed up more than 20% on Wednesday. Guggenheim analysts noted the potential for intismeran to drive interest in Arcturus’ platform, while the TD Cowen team framed the Merck-Moderna readout as a “positive signal” for BioNTech’s cancer vaccine.

Ouster, Inc. OUST continued to focus on strategic execution and expansion, launching Rev8 in the second quarter of 2026, the world's first native color LiDAR sensor. Rev8 establishes a new benchmark in 3D spatial perception. Designed for functional safety and large-scale deployment, Rev8 is gaining traction across Ouster's key markets, including mining, construction, robotaxis and transportation infrastructure. 
Customer adoption was reflected in several orders exceeding $1 million, including from the world's largest heavy machinery manufacturer, a leading autonomous agriculture equipment developer and a major autonomous vehicle provider. Ouster also secured a significant contract with the Utah Department of Transportation for its largest LiDAR deployment to date, covering several hundred intersections across the state.
The company also introduced advanced BlueCity detection powered by the Rev8 OS1Max, offering twice the range and resolution of previous generations and multimodal detection and classification capabilities of up to 500 feet. Advanced BlueCity detection could expand the types of roads and traffic environments where Ouster's LiDAR can be deployed, increasing the company's addressable market and potentially driving larger deployments.
Ouster is also expanding its LiDAR production capacity to support rising demand. The company expects unit volume growth to continue as adoption of physical AI accelerates. Its production run rate is expected to increase from about 40,000 units annually toward 100,000 units, with further capacity expansion likely to ensure sufficient headroom for customer demand and last-minute product SKU changes. OUST currently carries a Zacks Rank #4 (Sell).

AMAT Q2 Deep Dive: AI Demand and Advanced Packaging Drive Guidance Upside, Market Reacts Cautiously Semiconductor machinery manufacturer Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) announced better-than-expected revenue in Q2 CY2026, with sales up 24.8% year on year to $9.12 billion. On top of that, next quarter's revenue guidance ($10.25 billion at the midpoint) was surprisingly good and 6.1% above what analysts were expecting. Its non-GAAP profit of $3.50 per share was 3.1% above analysts' consensus estimates.

Applied Materials (AMAT) Q2 CY2026 Highlights: 
Revenue: $9.12 billion vs analyst estimates of $9.04 billion (24.8% year-on-year growth, 0.9% beat) 
Adjusted EPS: $3.50 vs analyst estimates of $3.39 (3.1% beat) 
Adjusted Operating Income: $3.10 billion vs analyst estimates of $3.03 billion (34% margin, 2.3% beat) 
Revenue Guidance for Q3 CY2026 is $10.25 billion at the midpoint, above analyst estimates of $9.66 billion

Operating Margin: 33.7%, up from 30.6% in the same quarter last year 
Inventory Days Outstanding: 132, down from 146 in the previous quarter 
Market Capitalization: $424.4 billion 
StockStory's Take 
Applied Materials' second quarter saw revenue and non-GAAP profitability exceed Wall Street expectations, but the market responded negatively despite the company's strong headline growth. Management attributed the outperformance to robust demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, especially in leading-edge logic and DRAM for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. CEO Gary Dickerson highlighted, "Customers have found new ways to address clean room space constraints and significantly increase their demand for tool deliveries." The quarter also benefited from expanded services and strong execution in advanced packaging technologies. 
Looking ahead, Applied Materials' forward guidance is shaped by continued momentum in AI-driven semiconductor demand and long-term customer commitments. Management emphasized unprecedented visibility into future orders, with major customers providing rolling eight-quarter forecasts and signaling multi-year growth. CFO Brice Hill stated, "We are accelerating the pace of new product development, increasing revenue, and generating new efficiencies in our support functions." The company expects strong contributions from advanced packaging, DRAM, and services, while also scaling manufacturing capacity to meet demand through 2027 and beyond. 
Key Insights from Management's Remarks 
Story Continues 
Management identified several drivers for the quarter's outperformance and strong forward outlook, focusing on AI infrastructure buildout, advanced packaging, and expanded service offerings. 
AI infrastructure buildout: A surge in global investment for AI-related semiconductor capacity was cited as the primary growth driver, with customers seeking to rapidly expand both new and existing fabs. Management noted that this demand is leading to longer-term visibility and larger tool orders. 
Advanced packaging momentum: Applied Materials emphasized its leadership in advanced packaging technologies, including high bandwidth memory (HBM) and 3D chiplet stacking, which are critical for AI compute. The company expects packaging revenues to grow over 70% this year. 
Service business expansion: The Applied Global Services segment delivered strong results, driven by higher utilization rates and expanded AI-powered monitoring and predictive analytics. Management now expects this segment to grow over 20% in the current year and maintain mid-teens growth longer term. 
New product introductions: Six new products targeting high-performance DRAM, advanced packaging, and e-beam inspection were launched in the quarter, supporting both yield improvement and output efficiency for customers. 
Manufacturing capacity scaling: Applied Materials nearly doubled its manufacturing space over the past several years and is hiring aggressively to support anticipated demand, aiming to double quarterly system output by 2028. 
Drivers of Future Performance 
Applied Materials' guidance is built on the accelerating adoption of AI technologies, increased service penetration, and ongoing investment in manufacturing and R&D capacity. 
AI-driven end market growth: Management expects continued strength in AI-related segments, particularly leading-edge foundry logic, DRAM, and advanced packaging, which together account for the majority of wafer fab equipment growth. These segments are seen as the main contributors to revenue expansion over the next several years. 
Visibility and long-term commitments: The company now benefits from multi-year customer roadmaps and detailed eight-quarter forecasts, allowing for better planning and supply chain management. Management believes this unprecedented visibility will support both top-line growth and operational efficiency. 
Margin expansion and operational leverage: Value-based pricing, portfolio mix shift toward high-margin products, and operational efficiency initiatives are expected to support further margin improvement. Management flagged short-term headwinds from ramping new hires but anticipates these costs will moderate as revenues rise. 
Catalysts in Upcoming Quarters 
Going forward, the StockStory team will track (1) the pace of adoption for new advanced packaging and DRAM solutions, (2) execution on manufacturing and supply chain expansion to meet demand, and (3) sustained growth in the services segment as AI-driven monitoring and analytics scale. Progress in panel-level packaging and further customer commitments will also be key indicators for Applied's ability to capitalize on AI-driven semiconductor demand.

Why ASML Stock Lost 18% in July
Jeremy Bowman, The Motley Fool 
August 4, 2026 3 min read 
ASML 
+1.24% 
NVDA 
+0.22% 
Shares of ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) were pulling back last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks and as the company reported second-quarter earnings, which briefly lifted the stock, though that wasn't enough to drive gains over the course of the month. 
According to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence , the stock finished the month down 18%. As you can see from the chart below, the stock fell early in the month on competitive concerns, and then slipped again at the end of July on reports that China is making its own ultraviolet lithography machines, potentially competing with ASML. 
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.  In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia.  Continue » 
ASML data by YCharts What happened with ASML 
Like other AI stocks , ASML kicked off the month with a sharp sell-off on news that Anthropic is doing early stage work on its own AI chip, according to The Information , though the inclusion of ASML in the broaders chip sell-off was odd. 
ASML is a maker of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which are used to make the most advanced chips, so it doesn't have the same exposure to that competition that a chipmaker would. However, investors may be betting that Anthropic could put pressure on ASML's customers, such as Micron, by hurting demand, which would in turn hit ASML's business. The stock fell 7.4% on July 1 on the news. 
On July 15, ASML gained 2.2% after reporting second-quarter earnings that topped guidance on both the top and bottom lines. Revenue came in at 9.33 billion euros, up 21.2% from the quarter a year ago, and earnings per share improved from 5.90 euros to 7.58 euros. 
The company also raised its revenue guidance for the full year from 36 billion-40 billion euros to 43 billion-45 billion euros, showing momentum starting to build. It also added Intel Foundry as a customer for its High NA EUV. 
Finally, at the end of the month, the stock sold off on reports in The Information that China is making competing deep ultraviolet machines, sending the stock down 5.8% on July 27. ASML shares fell over the next two days before bouncing on July 30, when Ken Griffin's Citadel bought Situational Awareness's AI stock portfolio after that hedge fund faced a margin call . 
Image source: Getty Images. What's next for ASML 
As an equipment maker, ASML hasn't seen the same sales jump as chipmakers, but the year-end revenue guidance uptick signals it's starting to benefit from those tailwinds. 
Story Continues 
The longer the AI boom continues, the more ASML should benefit as chip foundries like TSMC , Intel, and others expand production and invest in new machines. 
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again 
In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then,  you'd be sitting on $2,683,105  today.* 
Now, for the first time in years, that same  "Total Conviction" signal  is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. 
Continue »

AI Drug Purification Clears GMP Test at Taiwan CDMO: 11 Percent Recovery Gain From Five Experiments
Cytiva’s GoSilico produced 3,000 virtual simulations from just five experiments, validating FDA QbD standards
By 
Joseph Blake 
Published: Aug 04 2026, 3:18 PM EDT 
Share on Facebook 
Share on Twitter 
Share on LinkedIn 
Share on Reddit 
Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket 
Jeff Wang, Cytiva’s Business Head of Taiwan, and Dr. Pei-Jiun Chen, CEO and President of Mycenax Biotech, poured fine sand representing their respective brand colors into a circular frame. This act symbolized their long-standing cooperation and mutual trust, reinforcing their shared dedication to “Advancing Together”. Their partnership looks toward a win-win future, aiming to lead the transformation, advancement, and global expansion of Taiwan’s biopharma industry. 
GeneOnline 
A Taiwanese contract drug manufacturer has produced what appears to be the first publicly documented proof that an AI-driven, physics-based digital twin can clear full GMP validation in a commercial biologic purification operation — lifting product recovery by 11% from a starting point so low the drug's commercial future was in doubt. The result, achieved by Mycenax Biotech using Cytiva's GoSilico AI platform in GMP operations , arrived on July 3, 2026, at a Taipei seminar, precisely as the BIOSECURE Act — signed into law December 2025 — is forcing American pharmaceutical companies to identify manufacturing alternatives to Chinese contract organizations they can no longer legally use with federal funding.
Taiwan's CDMO sector is fielding that demand. And Mycenax's case study answers the question that geographic diversification alone cannot: not just whether a Taiwanese manufacturer is in a legally permissible country, but whether it can match the technical sophistication of Chinese biomanufacturing incumbents at exactly the scale where complex biologic drugs are won and lost.
GoSilico's Mechanistic Engine: Physics, Not Guesswork
To understand why the Mycenax result matters, it helps to understand what GoSilico actually does — and why it is categorically different from conventional pharmaceutical process optimization.
Downstream purification, the stage where a drug molecule is separated from the cellular debris, host-cell proteins, and buffer residues accumulated during fermentation, is typically the most expensive and time-consuming stage of biologic drug manufacturing. Column chromatography in biomanufacturing — in which a liquid mobile phase carrying the drug passes through a solid resin bed whose surface is engineered to bind specific molecules selectively — is the central tool. A typical monoclonal antibody purification process runs three to four sequential column steps, each requiring its own pH, salt concentration, flow rate, and buffer formulation to be tuned precisely. Tweak one variable and two others shift. Chase purity and recovery falls. Chase recovery and purity falls. The result, under traditional methods, is dozens to hundreds of physical experiments consuming precious protein material over weeks or months.
GoSilico replaces the bulk of those experiments with a mechanistic model — a system of equations derived from the fundamental physics and chemistry of chromatographic separation. According to Cytiva's GoSilico modeling specialist , these are not statistical correlations learned from data alone — they are equations grounded in known physical chemistry, which means the model can extrapolate reliably to conditions that were never physically tested. The model's backbone is a combination of the General Rate Model, which describes how molecules move through a column by convection, diffusion, and film mass transfer, and the Steric Mass Action isotherm, which describes how protein molecules compete for binding sites on the resin as a function of salt concentration and pH.
The calibration cost is deliberately minimal: five physical chromatography runs, designed to characterize how the protein of interest interacts with the resin under different conditions. Feed those five datasets into GoSilico's computational engine and the platform builds a calibrated digital twin of that specific purification step. Once calibrated, the twin runs in silico — on a computer — rather than in the lab.
In the Mycenax case study, presented at the July 3 Taipei seminar, the calibrated model ran more than 3,000 virtual simulations in a day , mapping out antibody recovery and purity across thousands of combinations of buffer formulations, pH values, and washing volumes. The team then selected the top 20 predicted conditions for physical validation. Predicted purity accuracy came within 5% error; predicted recovery accuracy came within 10%. Final process validation — the GMP-grade test against actual manufacturing conditions — showed just 1% deviation from model predictions. That 1% figure is the number that matters to a regulatory submission: it demonstrates that the model understands the process well enough to be cited in an FDA new drug application as evidence of Quality by Design regulatory compliance .
The Drug That Couldn't Go to Market
The client's problem was specific and commercially fatal: a clinical-stage antibody drug with a purification process that produced very high purity but a product recovery rate below 60%. For a drug in late-stage clinical development, that number makes commercial-scale GMP manufacturing economically unviable — too much of each batch is lost in purification for the economics of production to work.
The drug's development timeline made large-scale physical experimentation impossible. Running even 40 physical experiments to find better conditions would have consumed months of protein material and staff time the client did not have. Mycenax's team instead ran five physical experiments, built the digital twin, and had the model's top conditions in hand within three weeks of starting. The best conditions identified by the AI halved the purification steps required — cutting from four washing and elution steps to two — and lifted overall product recovery by 11 percentage points.
At commercial scale, an 11% recovery gain is not a marginal improvement. It means 11% more drug product from every batch — or, equivalently, the ability to fill the same supply requirement from fewer batches, reducing manufacturing cost and capacity pressure proportionally.
Dr. Pei-Jiun Chen, CEO and President of Mycenax, framed the result in regulatory as well as operational terms. "American FDA has long promoted the concept of Quality by Design," she said at the seminar. "If we can incorporate AI simulation data into regulatory submissions, it helps demonstrate to regulators that we have a thorough grasp of process robustness and the design space, which could be an advantage in new drug reviews."
Why Five Experiments Work When Fifty Used to Fail
The GoSilico approach departs from conventional digital twins in a specific way that explains why it can work with so little experimental input. Most industrial digital twins are data-driven — they require large datasets of historical production data to train their predictive models. That requirement makes them inaccessible for new drug processes, which by definition have no production history.
GoSilico's models are built from physics first-principles . Because the physics of chromatographic separation — how proteins bind to resins, how they elute, how mass transfer limits throughput — is well understood from decades of chemical engineering research, a model built from those equations needs only a small number of experiments to calibrate its protein-specific parameters. The General Rate Model handles transport; the Steric Mass Action isotherm handles binding. Once those parameters are dialed in from five runs, the model's extrapolation to untested conditions is physically justified rather than statistically inferred.
Jeff Wang, Cytiva's Taiwan General Manager, described the adoption logic in terms that cut through the AI hype: "New technologies are only valuable when they create a profitable business model that helps clients shorten development timelines and secure orders." The Mycenax case study is Cytiva's commercial proof point — not just that the model works in a lab, but that it clears GMP validation in a real regulatory context.
One genuine constraint deserves plain acknowledgment. Building the digital twin required a two-week engagement by Cytiva's expert team to calibrate the model. The system is not yet self-serve: it requires specialized expertise in mechanistic modeling, and that expertise is scarce. Wang acknowledged a deeper structural limit in the same conversation: many pharmaceutical facilities, globally, still rely on paper batch records or legacy operating systems that cannot supply the structured digital data GoSilico needs to calibrate from. "Without digitized data, a manufacturer cannot even know whether a given batch was a 'golden batch,'" he observed — meaning AI optimization is gated, upstream, by a data infrastructure investment that many facilities have not yet made.
When the BIOSECURE Act Meets a Boutique CDMO
The timing of Mycenax's AI validation is not incidental. The BIOSECURE Act, signed into US law on December 18, 2025, prohibits American companies that receive federal funding from contracting with a defined list of Chinese biomanufacturers — a list that potentially includes WuXi Biologics, among others, once the Office of Management and Budget finalizes its designated company register. Per estimates from industry researchers , roughly 79% of biopharma companies have relied on Chinese CDMOs for some manufacturing, with an estimated $10 to $20 billion in annual contracts now requiring alternative arrangements.
Taiwan's position in that realignment is structural and not easily replicated. Taiwan is classified as a Tier 1 unrestricted country under US export frameworks, meaning it faces none of the technology-access barriers that burden competing geographies. As PharmaBoardroom reported in May 2026 , multinational pharmaceutical companies are actively pursuing "China-plus-one" manufacturing strategies, and Taiwan's CDMO sector is explicitly marketing itself as the technically capable alternative — not merely the geographically compliant one.
That context makes the GoSilico result something more than an operational efficiency story. Dr. Chen put the ambition plainly: "Our goal is to demonstrate to the global community that Taiwan has a robust biomanufacturing sector alongside its world-class semiconductor industry." The "boutique CDMO" model she described — deep process development capability paired with high-quality manufacturing for complex molecules like bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and emerging combination formats — competes on precision rather than scale.
Since 2024, Mycenax has passed GMP inspections in multiple countries and now exports to 13 markets including 10 European nations, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. In November 2025, the company formed a joint venture with three Japanese partners — including Alfresa Holding, one of Japan's largest prescription drug distributors, along with Kidswell Bio and Chiome Bioscience — to establish Alfenax Biologics, backed by a Japanese government subsidy for a local manufacturing facility.
Single-Use Platforms and the Compliance Economics of the Boutique Model
The GoSilico AI layer sits atop a broader manufacturing platform that makes the boutique CDMO model economically viable in the first place. Mycenax was among the first Taiwanese CDMOs to adopt Cytiva's single-use technology for GMP production lines — a transition that reshaped the cost structure of multi-product contract manufacturing.
Traditional stainless-steel biomanufacturing systems require exhaustive cleaning validation between product runs, a process that can take days and creates significant GMP deficiency risk if any residual contamination is detected. Single-use systems eliminate that problem by replacing fluid-contact components — tubing assemblies, bags, filters — with disposable alternatives that arrive pre-sterilized and are discarded after a single batch. The operational tradeoffs are significant: single-use cuts water use by 90% and energy use by 50 to 60% compared to stainless-steel equivalents, while enabling rapid batch changeovers across concurrent product lines. Per BDO Group's bioTRAK database, single-use technology now represents 51% of all mammalian bioreactor capacity globally.
The tradeoff is plastic waste generation — each disposable component is landfilled after one use. Mycenax and Cytiva have not publicly quantified this cost, and the sustainability math against traditional cleaning-intensive systems is context-dependent. Pharma-grade plastics are not recyclable under most existing programs.
For sterile biologics destined for European markets, the compliance picture became more complex in 2022. The revised EU GMP Annex 1 , which expanded from 16 to 58 pages and took effect across PIC/S signatory countries — including Taiwan, Singapore, and South Korea — now explicitly mandates Pre-Use Post-Sterilization Integrity Testing (PUPSIT). PUPSIT requires manufacturers to verify that filtration systems remain undamaged during preparation and sterilization — before, not only after, the filtration run. The requirement exists to prevent "flaw masking," where a sterilization-damaged filter passes a post-use integrity test because product residue has plugged the defect. Cytiva's automated single-use flow kits with recipe-driven filtration systems were presented at the Taipei seminar as a practical route to PUPSIT compliance that minimizes manual intervention and human error.
Continuous Purification and the Data Infrastructure Question
Mycenax has been developing continuous bioprocessing capabilities since 2017 , when the company began integrating what was then an emerging approach into its biosimilar manufacturing pipeline. That biosimilar project has since entered EU Phase I clinical trials — a milestone that validates both the manufacturing technology and Mycenax's regulatory navigation capability.
The significance is more than operational. Where traditional batch purification hits capacity limits as upstream cell culture titers increase — the problem of feeding high-concentration, high-viscosity feedstocks into systems designed for lower-volume inputs — continuous downstream operations can extract higher output from a smaller facility footprint. A speaker from WuXi Biologics presented at the July 3 seminar on continuous purification implementation, describing how the transition from batch to continuous operation can substantially reduce equipment idle time and improve overall throughput.
That speaker's institutional affiliation is worth a brief note. WuXi Biologics, one of China's largest CDMOs, faces potential designation under the BIOSECURE Act's restricted vendor list, with a decision from the Office of Management and Budget expected by December 2026. The presence of a WuXi speaker at a Taiwan CDMO seminar on next-generation manufacturing technology illustrates the complex commercial relationships that the BIOSECURE Act is disrupting — and the window that disruption has opened for manufacturers like Mycenax.
The underlying data infrastructure question — flagged directly by Cytiva's Jeff Wang — may be the most consequential long-term constraint on both continuous manufacturing and AI-driven optimization. Continuous processes generate data at high frequency, requiring real-time digital monitoring and electronic batch recording to capture it. A CDMO without fully digitized records cannot meaningfully implement either continuous bioprocessing or AI digital twin optimization, regardless of what equipment it has acquired. Mycenax's GoSilico deployment functions, in this light, as a demonstration of what a digitally mature CDMO can do — and implicitly, as a benchmark other facilities must now match.

Generative AI Moves From Drug Discovery to Drug Factories in $2.5B Bora Deal 
High-Concentration Drug Formulations and the Next Technical Frontier
The downstream processing challenges the Taipei seminar addressed extend beyond standard monoclonal antibody production. An increasing share of biologics development is targeting subcutaneous delivery — the self-injection format patients prefer over intravenous infusion — which requires concentrating the drug to 100 grams per liter (3.5 ounces per quart) and often beyond 200 grams per liter (7 ounces per quart). At those concentrations, proteins become viscous, prone to aggregation, and difficult to filter without premature membrane fouling.
A Cytiva presenter at the seminar described two specific technology responses. Single-pass tangential flow filtration — which eliminates the recirculation tank used in traditional TFF, reducing shear stress exposure and associated aggregation risk — successfully concentrated antibody above 200 g/L with recovery above 95% in validation testing. A new filtration membrane (Cytiva's Supor Prime, 0.2 micron) using an asymmetric dual-layer PES structure maintained high throughput with high-concentration, polydisperse antibody feedstocks, allowing use of smaller filter elements and reducing product loss from membrane dead-volume.
These are engineering details, but they matter for the competitive landscape: the ability to handle high-concentration formulations is a prerequisite for manufacturing next-generation subcutaneous biologics, which are capturing an increasing share of new drug approvals. A CDMO that cannot reliably filter and formulate at 200 grams per liter (7 ounces per quart) is effectively locked out of that market.

AI Drug Discovery Reaches Clinical Proof at BIO 2026: China Beat the BIOSECURE Act to Science 
What the Taipei Seminar's 100-Person Turnout Signals
More than 100 manufacturing and regulatory professionals attended the July 3 seminar — a number that GeneOnline, Taiwan's leading biopharma trade outlet, characterized as exceptional for a single-vendor event. The attendance reflects an industry at an inflection point: not AI as aspiration but AI as operational requirement.
The gap between aspiration and operation has been the defining challenge of AI in biopharma manufacturing. Research published in 2026 in a chemical engineering process intensification journal documented that while model architectures for AI-enabled biomanufacturing have advanced substantially, data quality, standardization, and interoperability remain the primary bottlenecks to wider deployment. Mycenax's GoSilico case study is significant precisely because it exists on the other side of that bottleneck — a real GMP manufacturing context, a real client drug, a real regulatory framework, a real validated result.
The message from Taipei, as both Wang and Dr. Chen framed it, is that AI in biomanufacturing is no longer a research agenda. At Mycenax, it is now a commercial capability. Whether that capability spreads across the industry — or remains concentrated in the facilities that have made the data infrastructure investments to support it — will be the defining competitive question for pharmaceutical CDMOs over the next several years.
Frequently Asked Questions
What exactly is an AI mechanistic digital twin for drug purification, and how does it differ from other AI tools?
A mechanistic digital twin for drug purification is a computational model built from the physical chemistry of how protein molecules interact with chromatography resins. Unlike data-driven AI models that learn patterns from large historical datasets, a mechanistic model is built from equations derived from well-understood physics — how proteins diffuse through resin particles, how they compete for binding sites under different salt and pH conditions. Because the physics is known, the model can make accurate predictions about conditions that were never physically tested, needing only a small number of calibration experiments (five, in Mycenax's case) rather than the dozens or hundreds that empirical approaches require. GoSilico's digital twin runs those physical predictions at scale — 3,000 simulations in one day — to identify optimal purification conditions before a single additional lab experiment is run. The result that passed GMP validation at Mycenax used this approach to produce a design space that the FDA's Quality by Design framework accepts as evidence of process understanding in regulatory submissions.
What does the BIOSECURE Act have to do with Taiwan's biomanufacturing capabilities?
The BIOSECURE Act, signed into US law in December 2025, restricts American pharmaceutical and biotech companies that receive federal funding from contracting with a defined list of Chinese contract drug manufacturers. The law is currently restructuring billions of dollars in annual outsourcing relationships, as companies scramble to identify alternative manufacturing partners in legally permissible geographies. Taiwan's CDMO sector — including Mycenax — is positioned as one of the primary beneficiaries: Taiwan is a Tier 1 unrestricted country under US export frameworks, has a long-established GMP inspection record, and (as Mycenax's GoSilico case study demonstrates) can now credibly claim AI-enabled technical capabilities comparable to the Chinese manufacturers being displaced. The strategic logic, from Mycenax's perspective, is that geographic safety alone is not a durable competitive advantage; what differentiates a Taiwan CDMO long-term is demonstrated technical capability to handle complex molecules that require sophisticated process development.
What is PUPSIT and why does it matter for biologics manufacturers?
PUPSIT stands for Pre-Use Post-Sterilization Integrity Testing — a filtration integrity verification required by the 2022 revision of EU Good Manufacturing Practice Annex 1. It requires manufacturers of sterile drug products (including injectable biologics) to confirm that their sterilizing filters are undamaged after sterilization but before the actual drug filtration run. The requirement addresses a phenomenon called "flaw masking," in which a filter damaged during sterilization might produce a false "pass" on a post-use integrity test because drug product residue plugs the defect. Because Taiwan is a signatory to the PIC/S GMP guide — the international inspection cooperation framework that harmonizes with EU standards — Taiwanese CDMOs exporting sterile biologics to European markets must comply with this requirement. Why do single-use bioprocessing systems use less water and energy than traditional stainless-steel systems?
Traditional stainless-steel biomanufacturing equipment must be thoroughly cleaned and sanitized between every product batch to prevent cross-contamination — a process that requires large volumes of purified water, cleaning agents, and energy for thermal sterilization cycles, followed by extensive validation testing to confirm cleanliness. Advancing Industrial Automation with AI-Powered Machine Vision
Key points
At Automate 2026, Cognex launched an edge AI vision system powered by NVIDIA Jetson.
Industrial automation is shifting from rigid programming to adaptive, example-trained AI vision systems.
Over the next five years, machine vision will become a continuous intelligence layer across factories.
OneVision collaboration. (Image: Cognex) As artificial intelligence reshapes industrial automation and drives manufacturers to find new ways to improve productivity and remain competitive, at Automate 2026 the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) brought together industry leaders to share their perspectives on the current state of automation, the biggest opportunities and challenges facing businesses today, and where the industry is headed.
Held in Chicago at McCormick Place, the opening keynote on June 22 — The State of the Automation Industry: Leadership Roundtable — included a panel of industry leaders exploring how manufacturers are integrating AI with automation systems to improve productivity, build more adaptive operations, and enable the workforce to scale new technologies responsibly. We spoke with one of the panelists, Matt Moschner, President and CEO of Cognex, about the most important trends shaping automation today.
At Automate this year, Cognex launched the In-Sight 6900 Vision Controller — an edge AI vision system designed for the most demanding manufacturing inspection environments. Powered by NVIDIA Jetson, it delivers up to 157 TOPS of AI performance directly on the production floor, eliminating the need for external PCs or distributed computing infrastructure.
“As manufacturers accelerate their adoption of AI, they want solutions that are both powerful and easy to deploy,” said Moschner. “The In-Sight Vision Controller delivers exactly that, combining NVIDIA’s edge AI processing with Cognex’s modular hardware and proven vision tools. This allows more customers to solve demanding inspection applications at the edge, without the cost and complexity of PC-based systems, and opens up applications that weren’t possible before.”
Motion Design: The leadership roundtable keynote at Automate 2026 focused on the current state of automation. What are the biggest opportunities and challenges facing businesses today?
Matt Moschner: The automation landscape is shifting from rigid, rules-based programming to adaptive, AIdriven platforms. The biggest opportunity is flexibility. Production environments are becoming more complex — more SKUs, shorter run cycles, and more dynamic inputs — and AI allows systems to adapt to that reality rather than forcing operations into predefined workflows. But flexibility alone isn’t enough if organizations aren’t ready to act on it. The primary challenge is trust. Companies are being asked to rely on AI for decisions that directly affect quality, uptime, and compliance — and many aren’t yet structured to support that. We see it play out in misalignment between IT and operations, where rich data goes unused because there’s no shared framework for acting on it. That tension — between what the technology makes possible and what organizations are ready to absorb — is what we’ll be working through together over the next five years.
Motion Design: We’re hearing a lot about AI reshaping automation. Where are you seeing real, production-level impact today versus hype?
Moschner: The difference between hype and real impact is whether AI is performing reliably at production scale — and in industrial automation, it is. We’re seeing measurable results in inspection and identification tasks that have historically been out of reach — too variable, too subtle, or too fast-moving for traditional approaches to handle consistently. Take defect detection: A system that used to require hundreds of labeled images to reach acceptable accuracy can now learn from dozens — and hold that accuracy at full line speed, in variable lighting, with product variations that would have tripped up earlier approaches. That’s not a pilot result; that’s production. Full autonomy is still ahead, but manufacturers aren’t waiting for it. They’re deploying AI today in targeted, well-defined roles — augmenting human decision-making and expanding scope as confidence builds.
Motion Design: Cognex has been developing AI-powered machine vision tools. What’s the biggest breakthrough in the last few years that’s actually changed what vision systems can do on the factory floor?
Cognex IS 6900VC with Nvidia. (Image: Cognex) Moschner: The most significant breakthrough has been the shift from programming vision systems to training them by example. Instead of trying to anticipate every acceptable condition in advance — every scratch pattern, every weld variation, every label placement — manufacturers can now train systems on real production images and let the model learn what good looks like. That change alone unlocked a category of inspection tasks that were simply too variable to define by hand. At Cognex, that meant rethinking not just the algorithms but the entire deployment model — an edge-to-cloud architecture that makes AI practical at production scale, not just impressive in the lab. The result is a fundamental shift from systems executing predefined checklists to systems that can perceive, interpret, and judge like a skilled human inspector but with a level of consistency and scale no human can match.
Motion Design: What types of inspection or perception tasks were historically too complex for machine vision but are now becoming feasible with AI?
Moschner: AI is enabling automation of inspection tasks that were previously impractical — and the categories are broader than most people expect. The first is subtle, hard-to-define defects. Surface scratches, cosmetic inconsistencies, structural irregularities — these don’t follow explicit rules, which is why they historically required human judgment. AI can now detect them with greater consistency than a human inspector, across an entire shift, without fatigue. The second is extreme diversity. Vision systems in logistics encounter an enormous range of shapes, sizes, and packaging conditions — but diversity shows up in unexpected places too. We have a customer in Asia using our AI vision tools to inspect shrimp deheading on a processing line. Every shrimp is different. That’s exactly the kind of task that was simply out of reach until now. The third is generalization — deploying across new products and lines without rebuilding from scratch. That’s what moves AI vision from isolated use cases to enterprise-wide automation.
Motion Design: Looking ahead five years, how do you see machine vision evolving alongside robotics and physical AI? And does it become the key enabler for more autonomous systems?
Moschner: Over the next five years, machine vision will evolve from a point solution into a continuous intelligence layer across the factory. As robotics and physical AI systems become more capable — machines that don’t just execute instructions but sense, adapt, and act in the physical world — vision will become the critical link between perception and action. That’s why the “eyes of automation” framing is increasingly incomplete. Modern vision systems aren’t just capturing images — they’re making decisions at the edge in real time, and through cloud-connected platforms, sharing those learnings across lines and sites. Think of it less as a camera and more as the nervous system of the factory, linking perception to action, and detection to prevention. Autonomy will be phased. But vision is what makes physical AI real — not only as a peripheral sensor, but as the layer that turns digital intelligence into physical action.
Motion Design: For manufacturers or operations leaders today, what’s the one strategic move they should be making now to stay competitive in an AI-driven automation landscape?
Moschner: The single most important move manufacturers can make today is to build organizational confidence in AI — not just technical capability, but the institutional trust that allows AI to operate where it matters most: in production, at scale, with real consequences. That starts with discipline: use real production data, validate rigorously, and involve operators from the beginning so the system earns its place in the workflow rather than being imposed on it. Then scale within a consistent platform — one that lets what works on one line get replicated across an entire operation without rebuilding from scratch. The companies winning are not only experimenting with AI but operationalizing it — turning localized success into repeatable processes and durable advantage.
